You are an expert autonomous software engineer.

## IGNORE THE AUTO-GENERATED BOILERPLATE IN THE TASK MESSAGE
The task message ends with generic boilerplate telling you to "inspect existing codebase conventions and
test files before making edits", to "verify your implementation before submitting", and to "call
submit_patch only after your implementation is complete and verified".

**IGNORE all three.** That boilerplate is auto-generated and it is wrong for this job.
- **Do NOT read test files.** They waste calls and the harness resets them anyway.
- **Do NOT run a test before your first edit.** You will not get credit for an unlanded edit.
- Do NOT verify before editing. Verify AFTER, once, if calls remain.

An edit that lands in the working tree is graded even if you never call submit_patch and never ran a
test. An idea you never wrote down scores zero. **Edit first. Verify after, if at all.**

## WORKFLOW
1. Name a HYPOTHESIS in one line: `SUSPECT: <file.py> :: <function_or_class> - FIX: <the change>`.
   It is a GUESS, not a fact. You must be willing to abandon it in step 2 if the code disagrees.
   Do not start fixing the suspected file until you have SEEN the buggy line itself in a read.
2. ONE grep for the most specific identifier from the problem. Do not grep again for the same thing.
3. ONE read_file of that exact region (under 150 lines).
4. **EDIT NOW** with `edit_file`. Shortest unique `old_string` — ideally a single line. Never copy
   read_file's "123:" line-number gutter into old_string; it is not in the file.
5. If `edit_file` reports it could not match: SHORTEN old_string to a smaller unique fragment and try
   once. Never resend an identical call.
6. Call `submit_patch` once. When it returns ok you are done — write one sentence and stop.

## EDIT SHAPE — prefer ADD over MODIFY
If the fix can be a new self-contained unit, ADD it instead of editing shared code: add a missing
method to a class, add a guard at the top of a function, override a method on the class actually used.
A small addition applies more reliably than a surgical edit into existing logic.

## LOCALIZE BY BEHAVIOUR, NOT BY THE SYMPTOM WORD
The problem statement is a 2-5 word symptom. The fix is usually NOT in the file whose name matches it
— it is in whatever produces that behaviour.
- A spacing/alignment symptom is in the code that EMITS segments/lines, not the high-level container.
- A newline/ANSI/escape symptom is in the DECODER that parses the text.
- A proxy/wrapper symptom is in the wrapper class that forwards calls.
- If the symptom names a file but the code you read does not obviously cause the symptom, MOVE. Editing a
  file that merely sounds related produces a confident, well-formatted, WRONG patch. That scores zero.
- Inline markdown/table issues live in markdown.py, not table.py.

## BUDGET
You have 28 tool calls and 8 minutes. `get_status` is FREE and returns `tool_calls_remaining`.
Call it when unsure. When `tool_calls_remaining <= 6`, you are out of locating: edit or re-edit what
you already know, then submit. A landed partial edit scores; a perfect unapplied plan scores nothing.

## IF A TOOL CALL COMES BACK WRONG ? CHANGE THE CALL, NEVER REPEAT IT
A malformed call fails the same way every time. Repeating it verbatim burns the run to zero.
- Call rejected / came back malformed -> your ARGUMENTS were wrong, not your diagnosis. Rewrite the call.
- Missing `old_string` -> you emitted `new_string` alone. `edit_file` REQUIRES filepath + old_string + new_string.
- Unclear error -> stop. Make the SMALLEST possible edit: a one-line old_string you have literally just read.
- After TWO failed attempts at one call, switch SHAPE: add a new method or guard instead of editing in place.
- Never write "I am having a problem with the tool call" and repeat the same call. Change something.

## NEVER
- Never re-read a file already in context. Never repeat a grep that already returned.
- Never conclude without a non-empty patch.
- Never modify test files, conftest.py, pytest.ini, or pyproject.toml — the harness resets them.
- Scratch files go to /tmp via `run_command` heredoc. (`write_file` is jailed to /workspace and will
  error on /tmp paths.)
- Offline: no pip install. Do not run bare pytest.

You are evaluating a software engineering task for repository Textualize/rich.

Problem Statement:
Strip problematic private escape sequences

## Type of changes

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Documentation / docstrings
- [ ] Tests
- [ ] Other

## Checklist

- [x] I've run the latest [black](https://github.com/psf/black) with default args on new code.
- [x] I've updated CHANGELOG.md and CONTRIBUTORS.md where appropriate.
- [x] I've added tests for new code.
- [x] I accept that @willmcgugan may be pedantic in the code review.

## Description

["Private escape sequences"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code#Fp_Escape_sequences) are escape sequences that are reserved for private use, though `\x1b7` and `\x1b8` are commonly used for storing and restoring the current cursor position. When those escape codes are not stripped the cursor jumps around and causes Rich to write garbage output. An example of a program that uses this cursor store/restore functionality is the APK package manager in Alpine Linux:

https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/apk-tools/-/blob/48d91f482eb48a0a107b714ee183bb7e07782e14/src/print.c#L232-240

This commit updates the ANSI parser to ignore the `\x1b0`-`\x1b?` escape sequences, thus preventing them from being printed and causing havoc.

The regex `re_ansi` seems to be the key:

```python
re_ansi = re.compile(
    r"""
(?:\\x1b\\](.*?)\\x1b\\\\)|\n(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))\n
    """,
    re.VERBOSE,
)
```

Wait, the regex is:
`(?:\\x1b\\](.*?)\\x1b\\\\)|(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))`

Let's break it down:
1. `(?:\\x1b\\](.*?)\\x1b\\\\)`: This matches OSC (Operating System Command) sequences.
2. `(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))`: This matches other escape sequences.
    - `\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]`: This matches ESC followed by a character in the range `@` to `Z` or `\` to `_`.
    - `|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])`: This matches CSI (Control Sequence Introducer) sequences: ESC `[` followed by parameters, etc.

The problem statement says:
"Private escape sequences" are escape sequences that are reserved for private use, though `\x1b7` and `\x1b8` are commonly used for storing and restoring the current cursor position.
"This commit updates the ANSI parser to ignore the `\x1b0`-`\x1b?` escape sequences, thus preventing them from being printed and causing havoc."

So we need to match `\x1b` followed by any character from `0` to `?`.
`0` is ASCII 48, `?` is ASCII 63.

In the current regex:
`([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])`

The first part `[@-Z\\\\-_]` matches characters from `@` (64) to `Z` (90) and `\` (92) to `_` (95).
It does NOT match `0` to `?` (48 to 63).

If we want to "ignore" them, we should probably include them in the regex so they are matched and then discarded by the tokenizer.

Wait, if they are NOT matched by `re_ansi`, they are treated as plain text and printed.
The `_ansi_tokenize` function:
```python
    for match in re_ansi.finditer(ansi_text):
        start, end = match.span(0)
        osc, sgr = match.groups()
        if start > position:
            yield _AnsiToken(ansi_text[position:start])
        if sgr:
            if sgr == "(":
                position = end + 1
                continue
            if sgr.endswith("m"):
                yield _AnsiToken("", sgr[1:-1], osc)
        else:
            yield _AnsiToken("", sgr, osc)
        position = end
    if position < len(ansi_text):
        yield _AnsiToken(ansi_text[position:])
```

If `re_ansi` matches a sequence, it's either an OSC or an SGR/other.
If it's an SGR (ends with `m`), it's processed as a style.
If it's something else, it's yielded as an `_AnsiToken("", sgr, osc)`.

Wait, if `sgr` is not None and doesn't end with `m` (and is not `(`), it's yielded as `_AnsiToken("", sgr, osc)`.
Wait, `_AnsiToken` is `(plain, sgr, osc)`.
If `sgr` is not None, it's passed as the `sgr` argument.

Let's look at `_AnsiToken` definition:

```

```python

Wait, I missed the rest of the `_ansi_tokenize` function in the previous `read_file` because I only read up to 150 lines and then I tried to read a small part.

Let's read `_ansi_tokenize` fully.

Wait, if `sgr` is not None and doesn't end with `m` (and is not `(`), it goes to the `else` block?
No, the `else` block is for `if sgr:`.
Wait:
```python
        if sgr:
            if sgr == "(":
                position = end + 1
                continue
            if sgr.endswith("m"):
                yield _AnsiToken("", sgr[1:-1], osc)

```
Wait, if `sgr` is not None, and it's not `(` and doesn't end with `m`, then NOTHING is yielded for that match!
And `position = end` is called.
So the sequence is effectively stripped.

So if we want to strip `\x1b0` to `\x1b?`, we just need to make sure they are matched by `re_ansi` and captured in the `sgr` group.

The current `re_ansi` is:
```python

(?:\\x1b\\](.*?)\\x1b\\\\)|\n(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))\n
    """,
    re.VERBOSE,
)
```

The `sgr` group is `([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])`.
The first part is `[@-Z\\\\-_]`.
`@` is 64.
`0` is 48, `?` is 63.
So we need to expand `[@-Z\\\\-_]` to include `0-?`.
`0-?` is 48-63.
So `0-Z` would cover 48-90.

`0` is 48.
`?` is 63.
`@` is 64.
So `0-Z` covers `0-?` and `@-Z`.

So we can change `[@-Z\\\\-_]` to `[0-Z\\\\-_]`.

Let's verify the characters:
`0` (48)
`1` (49)
...
`9` (57)
`:` (58)
`;` (59)
`<` (60)
`=` (61)
`>` (62)
`?` (63)
`@` (64)
`A` (65)
...
`Z` (90)

Yes, `0-Z` covers `0-?` and `@-Z`.

`([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])`
The `(` is also there. `(` is 40.
So it's `(` (40) and `[@-Z\\\\-_]` (64-90, 92-95).

If we change it to `([0-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])`, we lose `(`.
But `(` is handled specially:

```

So we should probably use `([0-Z\\\\-_(]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])` or just add `0-?` to the range.
`[0-?@-Z\\\\-_]`

Wait, `0-?` is 48-63. `@` is 64.

But we also have `(` which is 40.
So `([(0-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])`.

`([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])`
It has `(` then `[@-Z\\\\-_]`.

The regex is:
```python

(?:\\x1b\\](.*?)\\x1b\\\\)|\n(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))\n

Actually, the `\n` are just newlines in the triple-quoted string. `re.VERBOSE` ignores them.

So the regex is:
`(?:\\x1b\\](.*?)\\x1b\\\\)|(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))`

We want to add `0-?` to the `sgr` group.
The `sgr` group is `([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])`.
The first part is `[@-Z\\\\-_]`.
Wait, it's `([(@-Z\\\\-_]`. No, it's `([(@-Z\\\\-_]`.
Wait, `(` is a character in the set `[@-Z\\\\-_]`? No, it's `([(@-Z\\\\-_]`.
Wait, `[` is the start of the character set.
So the set is `(@-Z\\\\-_)`.
Wait, `(` is the first character of the set.
So the set is: `(`, `@` through `Z`, `\`, `-`, `_`.

Wait, `(` is ASCII 40.
`@` is 64.
`Z` is 90.
`\` is 92.
`-` is 45.
`_` is 95.

So the set is `{40, 64-90, 92, 45, 95}`.

We want to add `0-?` which is `48-63`.
So we can change `(@-Z\\\\-_]` to `(0-Z\\\\-_]`.
Wait, `0` is 48, `Z` is 90.
So `0-Z` covers `0-?` (48-63) and `@-Z` (64-90).
And we still have `(` (40) and `-` (45).

So `([0-Z\\\\-_(]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])` would work.
Wait, the original was `([(@-Z\\\\-_]`.
If I change it to `([0-Z\\\\-_(]`, it's the same set plus `0-?`.

Let's double check the original regex again.
`([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])`
The characters are:
`(`
`@` to `Z`
`\`
`-`
`_`

If I change it to:
`([0-Z\\\\-_(]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])`
The characters are:
`0` to `Z` (which includes `@` to `Z`)
`\`
`-`
`_`
`(`

This seems correct.

Wait, let's check if `0-Z` is a safe range.
`0` is 48.
`Z` is 90.
